title: Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. MNR (1988 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: TCC case examining whether shop-floor manufacturing improvements constituted systematic investigation under SR&ED rules.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; court held trial-and-error tinkering without controlled experiments and recorded analysis is not SR&ED.
summary: Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. MNR (1988, Tax Court of Canada) is a foundational SR&ED decision for Canadian taxpayers claiming scientific research incentives under the Income Tax Act. Judge Sarchuk held that eligibility requires cogent evidence of a systematic investigation—controlled experiments, highly accurate measurements and testing theories against empirical evidence—so undocumented trial-and-error engineering does not qualify.
metaDescription: Examine the 1988 TCC decision in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363) regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit eligibility rules.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Sass Manufacturing Limited v. Minister of National Revenue, 88 DTC 1363, [1988] 1 C.T.C. 2524, [1988] T.C.J. No. 409 (T.C.C.), delivered by Judge Sarchuk on May 9, 1988, stands as one of the foundational jurisprudential authorities governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives in Canada. Prior to the codification of the five-criteria judicial framework in later Tax Court jurisprudence, Sass Manufacturing established the definitive evidentiary standard separating eligible experimental development from ineligible routine engineering, custom machine fabrication, and empirical trial-and-error problem-solving. Over three decades after its pronouncement, the decision remains explicitly embedded within the Canada Revenue Agency's (CRA) Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (CRM) and serves as the primary judicial precedent cited by the Crown to disallow claims lacking contemporaneous empirical measurement and controlled experimentation.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Technical Undertaking

Sass Manufacturing Limited, an Ontario-based custom machinery manufacturer and steel fabricator operating out of Chatham, Ontario, appealed reassessments issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") with respect to its 1981, 1982, and 1983 taxation years. The appeals raised two distinct statutory disputes under the Income Tax Act (the "Act"): first, the disallowance of an inventory allowance deduction claimed pursuant to paragraph 20(1)(gg) of the Act, where the Court held that the appellant had failed to adduce clear and cogent evidence as to the nature of each individual contract and therefore failed to demonstrate that the work in process of its "supply and install" contracts was held for sale in the ordinary course of its business, allowing the appeal only in respect of certain "supply only" contracts; and second, the disallowance of an additional allowance for scientific research claimed pursuant to section 37.1 of the Act and an additional Investment Tax Credit (ITC) claimed pursuant to subsection 127(5) of the Act in respect of expenditures alleged to have been incurred in the 1982 and 1983 taxation years, read in conjunction with section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations").

The technical project underlying the SR&ED dispute centered on the fabrication and testing of a prototype machine, the "Auto-Piper", conceived by George Bruinsma, a professional engineer and President of Auto Piper Sewer Systems Inc., as a means of resolving a problem in the laying of asbestos concrete sewer pipe (the appellant had also claimed $3,821 for a prototype "in-drain" pump in 1983, but abandoned that portion of its appeal at the outset of the hearing). Specifically, the appellant's management believed that, if the design was successful, the machine would reduce the cost of installing concrete sewer pipe and thereby take advantage of the lower cost of concrete pipe, which would make the machine marketable; the respondent's expert described the technological advancement sought as reducing the labour content in laying concrete sewer pipe to the point where its installed cost could compete with plastic sewer pipe. The machine was designed to travel over a pre-dug trench, deposit a gravel bed on the bottom, place the sewer pipe in the trench, line up and butt-connect the pipes, correct pipe butting and centring by means of a closed-circuit television system viewed by the machine operator, and finally deposit and tamp gravel around and over the pipe, with a laser-guided system to control pipe level as one novel design feature.

On December 4, 1981, Sass Manufacturing entered into an agreement with Bruinsma to fabricate this prototype unit, under which all design engineering, detailed drawings, and mechanical parts were to be provided by Bruinsma as owner, Sass Manufacturing was to perform all fabrication and management at a rate of $23.50 per man-hour, and special financial terms applied whereby the total cost was payable in three interest-free instalments of one-third each (60 days, six months, and not more than one year after the date of invoice), accompanied by a covenant whereby Sass Manufacturing agreed not to fabricate the machine for any other potential customers without Bruinsma's consent. In advancing its appeal before the Tax Court of Canada, the taxpayer contended that its involvement in the Auto-Piper project fell within the "development" category of Regulation 2900, namely the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating a new device or product, and that its lack of written records should be viewed in the context of a small company whose limited staff and time precluded attention to such detail; the specific uncertainties discussed at trial (such as whether the trench walls would support the machine, whether the concrete pipe sections could be properly aligned and butted by an operator viewing them on closed-circuit television, and the tamping mechanism's failure to perform properly as initially constructed) were identified in the report of the respondent's expert witness.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister challenged the characterization of the prototype sewer pipe-laying machine project on both substantive technical grounds and evidentiary insufficiency. The Crown maintained that the taxpayer's activities did not constitute "scientific research" within the meaning of Regulation 2900(1), asserting that the expenses associated with the manufacture and testing of the Auto-Piper were not expenses incurred on account of scientific research and experimental development and, in the alternative, that even if they were, they were not incurred by the appellant in the 1982 taxation year but rather by the customer for whom the prototype was manufactured. Through the evidence of its expert witness, R. Garth Doel, a mechanical engineering graduate of Queen's University, the Respondent showed that, although the prototype was tested at the appellant's premises and in the field and some changes and adjustments were made, the systematic application of the scientific method was not performed, no records were kept of test observations or of machine modifications and the reasons for them, and the prototype as designed could not handle difficult soil conditions. Furthermore, Doel's report concluded that no one assigned to the project from Sass Manufacturing had proper qualifications, either by education or experience, to carry out the research, that no hypothesis for research appears to have been postulated, and that there were no test reports and no data collected and preserved, while the Respondent emphasized that the prototype was custom-built for a customer under a fabrication contract; notably, the expenditures were not claimed or reported as qualifying scientific research expenses in the income tax returns originally filed by the appellant.
The Governing Statutory Framework

During the 1982 and 1983 taxation years for which scientific research expenditures were at issue in Sass Manufacturing, the general deduction for scientific research expenditures resided in section 37 of the Act and the additional allowance actually claimed by the appellant resided in section 37.1 of the Act, while Regulation 2900, which applied for the purposes of Part XXIX of the Regulations and paragraphs 37(7)(b) and 37.1(5)(e) of the Act, defined the expression "scientific research" for those purposes. Subsequent legislative amendments consolidated the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" directly into subsection 248(1) of the Act, retaining the substantive architecture of former Regulation 2900(1) while pairing expenditure pool deductions under subsection 37(1) with Investment Tax Credits governed by subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act.

Under Regulation 2900(1) (and its modern counterpart in subsection 248(1) of the Act), eligible SR&ED is strictly defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory definition bifurcates qualifying work into three primary categories: paragraph (a) encompasses basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph (b) covers applied research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph (c) governs development, which Regulation 2900 as applied in Sass Manufacturing defined as the use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes (the modern subsection 248(1) definition instead refers to experimental development, namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto).

For experimental development claims, the modern statute permits the inclusion of supporting activities—such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—under paragraph (d) (Regulation 2900 as quoted in Sass Manufacturing listed engineering or design, operations research, mathematical analysis or computer programming and psychological research, where undertaken directly in support of basic research, applied research or development), provided those activities are commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, the modern statutory regime explicitly excludes commercial and routine engineering activities under paragraphs (e) through (k), specifically disqualifying market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or humanities; prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
The Court's Final Holding

Judge Sarchuk dismissed Sass Manufacturing Limited's appeal on the scientific research issue, allowed the appeal in part only in respect of the inventory allowance claimed on certain "supply only" contracts, and otherwise confirmed the reassessments. In a landmark pronouncement at page 1371 (paragraph 48 of the reasons for judgment), the Court articulated the legal threshold that every Canadian taxpayer must surmount to establish SR&ED eligibility:

"In my view Regulation 2900 requires an appellant to adduce cogent evidence of such investigation or search. Systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and of highly accurate measurements and involves the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence."

The Tax Court held that the evidence fell far short of establishing any systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis, observing that scientific research would surely include repeatable experiments in which the steps, the various changes made, and the results are carefully noted; independently, the Court held that the appellant had not made qualified expenditures in the 1982 taxation year because the project expenses were paid on behalf of its customer Bruinsma, who was billed for them, and the appellant acquired no rights to the concept or design. Because key design and testing decisions were made on what the appellant's own witness described as an engineering hunch basis, no records of discussions, decisions, tests, or modifications were kept, and whatever limited records existed were discarded when the project was abandoned in 1983, the work fell below the statutory threshold of a "systematic investigation or search" under Regulation 2900 and was consequently ineligible for the section 37.1 additional allowance and subsection 127(5) ITCs.
Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of Judge Sarchuk's ruling reveals that the taxpayer's disqualification did not stem from a single isolated oversight, but rather from a combination of interlocking legal and technical dimensions: the absence of a structured methodology of experimentation (the decisive ground), a complete lack of contemporaneous records, the appellant's position as a custom fabricator that incurred the expenditures on behalf of a customer without acquiring any rights to the concept or design, and, as shown by the unchallenged evidence of the respondent's expert, the absence of properly qualified personnel and of any thorough engineering analysis of the uncertainties encountered.
Conflation of Functional Malfunction with Technological Uncertainty

A further substantive weakness in Sass Manufacturing lay in the taxpayer's inability to show, through any recorded engineering analysis, which of the uncertainties encountered were genuine scientific or technological uncertainties rather than functional problems that a reasonable amount of engineering analysis should have foreseen; although Judge Sarchuk decided the issue on the absence of a systematic investigation rather than on the existence of uncertainty, the respondent's expert addressed this distinction in detail. In his report, the respondent's expert identified the elements of uncertainty in the project, including whether the walls of the trench would support the machine, whether the concrete pipe sections could be properly aligned and butted by an operator viewing them by closed-circuit television, whether the pipe alignment mechanism would perform properly, and uncertainties that arose when the tamping mechanism did not perform properly as initially constructed and in the winch mechanism for telescoping the gravel insertion tube, rating the overall level of uncertainty as moderate.

From a Canadian tax law perspective, the mere fact that a prototype machine fails to operate as intended, or that its builder is uncertain whether a mechanical assembly will function upon initial fabrication, does not establish technological uncertainty. As subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence building directly upon the foundation of Sass Manufacturing clarified, implicit in the concept of technical risk or uncertainty is the requirement that the obstacle cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field. In Sass Manufacturing, the respondent's expert considered that a reasonable amount of engineering analysis should have foreseen the problems with the tamping mechanism and the winch mechanism, while acknowledging that the loadings on various components, the functional performance of several components, and the action of the soil in the trench could not be determined by analysis alone, and that the interaction of the machine's many components was not readily predictable. The taxpayer adduced no evidence that any thorough engineering analysis had been carried out, and no evidence was adduced as to the basis upon which Bruinsma evolved the design, so the record could not show why standard engineering analysis was incapable of predicting the behaviour of the tamping mechanism. Instead of documenting how the genuine uncertainties identified by the expert were investigated, the taxpayer was left to rely on the general assertion that the project constituted development, supported only by the layman's testimony of a witness who was not directly involved in the project.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Repeatability

The decisive deficiency identified by Judge Sarchuk was the complete absence of a "systematic investigation or search" carried out by means of experiment or analysis. After the completed prototype was tested at the appellant's premises in 1982, several problems were disclosed, some changes and adjustments were made, and a further field test was conducted at which the prototype, running into varying strata of soil and levels of gravel that kept collapsing into the trench, proved unable as designed to handle difficult soil conditions; the machine never achieved acceptable functionality, and in 1983 the project was abandoned and the prototype salvaged for its component parts. The Court found no evidence of any systematic investigation in the changes and adjustments made, and the respondent's expert noted that it was not possible to trace the appellant's trial steps and progress; undocumented modification of this kind, colloquially known as "cut-and-try" or trial-and-error engineering, does not satisfy Regulation 2900.

Judge Sarchuk established that a "systematic investigation" legally requires three interdependent methodological elements: the formulation of a scientific or technological theory (hypothesis), the execution of controlled experiments where variables are isolated and manipulated, and the collection of highly accurate measurements to test the theory against empirical evidence. Furthermore, Judge Sarchuk expressly stated that scientific research would include repeatable experiments in which the steps, the various changes made, and the results are carefully noted, and as later courts observed when citing Sass Manufacturing, Judge Sarchuk's framework imposes a strict "repeatability requirement". In practical terms, an investigation is demonstrably systematic when an independent, competent professional can review the recorded steps, changes, and results, as the respondent's expert attempted and was unable to do in this case. In Sass Manufacturing, the appellant could produce no hypothesis, no test reports, no records of test observations or of machine modifications and the reasons for them, no photographs of the prototype or of the problems encountered, and no data useful for further work, so that there was absolutely no statistical or test-result basis upon which to determine where the project left off. In the absence of any record of controlled experiments or measurements, the taxpayer's modifications were legally indistinguishable from routine trial-and-error fabrication.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Lack of Qualified Personnel

In Canadian tax litigation, the initial onus rests squarely upon the appellant to demolish the Minister's assumptions of fact by adducing "cogent evidence". The record disclosed two glaring evidentiary voids, one noted by Judge Sarchuk and the other established by the unchallenged evidence of the respondent's expert, that undermined the credibility of the taxpayer's claim. First, the appellant failed to produce contemporaneous technical records generated during the 1982 taxation year that evidenced a research protocol, analytical calculations, test logs, or empirical data; no records were kept of the discussions and decisions among Bruinsma, the general manager Van Giessen and the president Metro Sass, and what limited records may have existed were discarded when the project was abandoned. As the reasons in Sass Manufacturing disclose, the appellant conceded that its initial intention was to build a prototype based on Bruinsma's drawings and nothing more and that Bruinsma was merely another customer, and the expenditures were not claimed as scientific research in its original returns; in the words later used to describe this record, the appellant "was not even thinking about SRED" while fabricating the machine, and characterized the project as scientific research only after the fact. Without contemporaneous documentation recording hypotheses, test parameters, and outcomes as they occurred, the only oral testimony offered at trial on the project came from the appellant's comptroller, Robert Sass, who was not directly involved in the project and could offer little more than a layman's view, while the general manager, in whose head the remaining knowledge resided, did not testify; such evidence could not satisfy the cogent evidence standard.

Second, the respondent's expert, whose conclusions the Court noted were not seriously challenged on cross-examination, identified a critical human resource deficiency: "No one assigned to this project from Sass Manufacturing Ltd." had proper qualifications, either by education or experience, to carry out this research (the expert noted that Bruinsma, P.Eng., may have had suitable education and experience, and that R.M. Pow Consulting Engineers, which prepared the detailed drawings, would have been qualified but disclaimed responsibility for the concept and attended none of the field tests). While the Income Tax Act does not impose a strict statutory requirement that SR&ED personnel hold university degrees or professional engineering (P.Eng.) designations, the absence of formally trained engineering personnel heavily undermined the taxpayer's assertion that the obstacles encountered exceeded "routine engineering". When personnel lacking formal engineering training encounter difficulty designing a tamping mechanism, the resulting uncertainty is frequently "subjective uncertainty"—a gap in the specific worker's personal knowledge—rather than "objective technological uncertainty," which exists only when the solution is not generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.
Contractual Structure and Commercial Production Exclusions

The contractual and financial arrangements governing the prototype unit further compromised the appellant's legal position. The written agreement of December 4, 1981 between Sass Manufacturing and its customer, George Bruinsma, stipulated that "for the fabrication of this prototype unit, Sass Manufacturing Limited agrees to provide the following special financial terms: (i) one third of total cost 60 days after..." and further bound the taxpayer to an exclusivity clause: "Sass Manufacturing Limited hereby agrees not to fabricate this machine for any..." other party.

Judge Sarchuk relied on this contractual architecture to hold that the appellant had not made qualified expenditures in the 1982 taxation year, and under the modern regime the same architecture would create two severe statutory vulnerabilities. First, under Regulation 2900(1)(i) (now paragraph 248(1)(i) of the Act), "the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process" is explicitly excluded from SR&ED. Although the Court did not apply this exclusion (the respondent's expert considered that the project had no commercial content because the prototype was never completed), the contract was structured as a custom fabrication engagement under which the appellant built a prototype to Bruinsma's specifications at a man-hour rate with deferred payment terms and an exclusivity covenant, so that the prototype served as a customer deliverable rather than an experimental test-bed owned by the appellant. Second, under subsection 127(18) of the Act, a taxpayer's qualified expenditures (as defined in subsection 127(9)) are reduced by any contract payment received or receivable where the research is performed for or on behalf of another person. In the actual decision, Judge Sarchuk found that the project expenses incurred in 1982, although paid by the appellant, were paid on behalf of its customer Bruinsma and billed to him, that the appellant had no right to Bruinsma's concept or to the results of his research and investigation, that its sole entitlement was to be paid under the contract, and that there was no evidence that its later seizure of the prototype under a lien action gave it any rights to the concept or design; the expenditures were therefore not qualified expenditures made by the appellant.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial SR&ED requirement established in Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. against the specific deficiencies exhibited by the taxpayer and the corresponding standard of proof demanded by the Tax Court of Canada and the CRA.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: Objective Technological Uncertainty
Regulation 2900(1)(c) (development); ITA s. 248(1)(c) ("achieving technological advancement")

Did not document any engineering analysis of the uncertainties identified by the respondent's expert (rated moderate); the expert considered that the tamping and winch problems should have been foreseen by a reasonable amount of engineering analysis, although the Court decided the case on the absence of a systematic investigation.
The taxpayer must prove through baseline engineering analysis that the obstacle could not be resolved using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field.
Formulation of Testable Hypotheses
Regulation 2900(1); ITA s. 248(1) ("by means of experiment or analysis")

Built the prototype to Bruinsma's concept and R.M. Pow's detailed drawings; no hypothesis for research appears to have been postulated, and no evidence was adduced as to the basis on which the design was evolved.
The claimant must adduce evidence of explicit theories formulated prior to experimentation that propose a causal scientific relationship aimed at eliminating the technological uncertainty.
Systematic Investigation & Controlled Experiments
Regulation 2900(1); ITA s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search")
Made undocumented changes and adjustments after in-plant and field tests, with decisions taken on an engineering hunch basis and no evidence that systematic test procedures were established.

"Systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments... and involves the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence", which would include repeatable experiments in which the steps, the various changes made and the results are carefully noted.
Highly Accurate Measurements & Repeatability
Regulation 2900(1); ITA s. 248(1); Sass Manufacturing at p. 1371

Kept no test reports or records of test observations, and collected and preserved no data; the problems encountered were described only qualitatively (e.g., the tamping mechanism did not perform properly as initially constructed).

The taxpayer must adduce evidence of highly accurate measurements recorded in repeatable experiments in which the steps, the changes made and the results are carefully noted (later jurisprudence speaks of established and objective principles of scientific measure).
Contemporaneous Cogent Evidence
ITA s. 230(1); Regulation 2900(1); Sass Manufacturing at p. 1371

Produced no contemporaneous test logs, engineering calculations, or systematic research protocols; whatever limited records existed were discarded when the project was abandoned, and the expenditures were not claimed as scientific research in the returns originally filed.

Regulation 2900 requires an appellant to adduce cogent evidence of a systematic investigation or search; in practice this means records made as the work proceeds, linking specific expenditures and labour hours to systematic experiments.
Competent Technical Personnel
Judicial criteria bridging Regulation 2900(1) and subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence

"No one assigned to this project from Sass Manufacturing Ltd." had proper qualifications, either by education or experience, to carry out the research, per the unchallenged evidence of the respondent's expert (Bruinsma, P.Eng., may have had suitable qualifications, but no record of them was available).
Project governance must involve or be directed by personnel competent in the relevant field of science or technology to prove that uncertainties are objective rather than subjective skill gaps.
Separation from Commercial Production & Contract Exclusions
ITA s. 37.1 (qualified expenditure made by the taxpayer), as applied in Sass Manufacturing; Regulation 2900(1)(i); ITA s. 248(1)(i), s. 37(1), ss. 127(9) and 127(18)

Custom-fabricated a prototype to its customer's specifications under special payment terms (three one-third instalments) and an exclusivity covenant; the 1982 expenses were paid on the customer's behalf and billed to him, and the appellant acquired no rights to the concept or design.

The Court held that expenses paid on behalf of a customer and billed to it are not qualified expenditures made by the taxpayer where the taxpayer has no rights to the concept or results; under the modern regime, experimental development must also be segregated from commercial production deliverables, and contracts must preserve intellectual property rights and avoid "contract payment" reductions.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how modern Canadian taxpayers and technical tax advisors can operationalize the legal principles of Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., the following two industry case studies examine commercial engineering projects that exhibit the exact vulnerabilities identified by Judge Sarchuk. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, contract law, and experimentation tracking to satisfy subsection 248(1), section 37, and subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Heavy Civil Infrastructure & Automated Trenching Robotics
Initial Vulnerable Project Posture (The Sass Manufacturing Trap)

A mid-sized Ontario heavy equipment manufacturer ("TrenchTech Corp.") enters into an agreement with a municipal utility contractor to build a custom, tractor-mounted automated trench-shoring and high-density polyethylene (HDPE) conduit-bedding machine. Under the contract, the utility contractor agrees to pay one-third of the shop fabrication costs 60 days after delivery and the remaining balance after successful field operation, in exchange for an exclusivity covenant prohibiting TrenchTech Corp. from fabricating the machine for any competing contractor.

During fabrication and field trials, TrenchTech's shop foremen—who are experienced millwrights and welders but hold no formal mechanical or geotechnical engineering credentials—discover that the hydraulic vibratory tamping shoes do not perform properly to achieve uniform soil compaction under wet clay conditions, and the automated rollers frequently jam when aligning and butting curved HDPE pipe segments. The shop team spends eight months modifying hydraulic valve pressures, welding stiffer gussets onto the tamping arms, and changing roller geometries by trial and error until the machine passes field inspection. At year-end, TrenchTech files Form T661 claiming $650,000 in SR&ED labour, materials, and overhead. Upon audit, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) issues a proposal letter disallowing the entire claim, citing Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363) on the grounds that the work was routine trial-and-error mechanical debugging performed by non-engineers on a commercial production unit subject to contract payment reductions.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Technical Oversight

To overcome the finding of the respondent's expert witness in Sass Manufacturing, which went unchallenged before Judge Sarchuk, that "no one assigned to this project from Sass Manufacturing Ltd." had proper qualifications, either by education or experience, to carry out the research, TrenchTech must establish formal technical governance before experimental work commences. TrenchTech assigns a licensed Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) specializing in terramechanics and hydraulic control systems to serve as Principal Investigator. Prior to any metal cutting or shop fabrication, the P.Eng. conducts a documented "Standard Practice Baseline Assessment". This baseline document reviews published geotechnical literature, finite element analysis (FEA) models, and standard hydraulic design equations to establish why competent professionals in the field cannot predict the coupled dynamic interaction between high-frequency hydraulic tamping actuators and thixotropic (shear-thinning) wet clay soils without inducing localized soil liquefaction and upward pipe displacement. By anchoring the project in an objective limitation of terramechanics rather than a simple mechanical jam, TrenchTech transforms a functional malfunction into an objective Technological Uncertainty under subsection 248(1) of the Act.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contractual Terms and IP Ownership

To eliminate the commercial production exclusion under paragraph 248(1)(i) and prevent the customer's payments from being characterized as an SR&ED-reducing contract payment under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the Act, legal counsel must sever the experimental development phase from the commercial equipment sale. Rather than executing a single prototype fabrication contract with deferred commercial payment terms and customer exclusivity, TrenchTech restructures the commercial arrangement into two legally distinct instruments. First, TrenchTech executes a Collaborative Field-Testing Access Agreement under which TrenchTech retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all intellectual property, experimental sub-assemblies, and design data, while the utility contractor provides access to its trenching site solely as an in-kind testing environment without paying any reimbursement toward the experimental development phase. Second, TrenchTech executes a separate, subsequent Commercial Supply Option granting the customer an option to purchase a commercial unit at fair market value under a distinct commercial invoice only after the technological uncertainties are resolved and the experimental phase is formally closed. Furthermore, during the experimental phase, TrenchTech does not build a complete commercial tractor unit as a single SR&ED deliverable; instead, it isolates the experimental prototype sub-assembly (the variable-frequency vibratory tamping and alignment module), ensuring that only engineering, design, and testing costs commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the experimental module are claimed under paragraph 248(1)(d).
Step 3: Implementing Controlled Experimentation and Quantitative Measurement Protocols

To satisfy Judge Sarchuk's mandate that "systematic investigation connotes the existence of controlled experiments and of highly accurate measurements and involves the testing of one's theories against empirical evidence", TrenchTech replaces ad hoc shop modifications with a structured, five-stage hypothesis-testing protocol. Prior to each iteration, the P.Eng. formulates and logs an explicit causal hypothesis proposing that decoupling the tamping actuator amplitude (2 to 8 mm) from excitation frequency (20 to 60 Hz) via closed-loop electro-hydraulic proportional damping will prevent pore-water pressure buildup exceeding 15 kPa in saturated cohesive clay, thereby achieving 95% Standard Proctor Density without inducing vertical pipe displacement exceeding 5 mm. Rather than altering roller geometry, hydraulic pressure, and tamping shoe shape simultaneously in an uncontrolled field trench, TrenchTech constructs an instrumented test cell containing standardized soil beds with controlled moisture content (18%, 24%, and 30% gravimetric water content), altering only one independent variable (excitation frequency) per test series while holding hydraulic downforce constant. Visual inspection ("did not perform properly") is replaced by calibrated instrumentation: TrenchTech installs piezo-resistive pore-water pressure transducers in the bedding zone, triaxial accelerometers on the tamping shoe, laser displacement sensors tracking pipe alignment to ±0.5 mm accuracy, and nuclear densometer readings measuring post-tamping soil compaction.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation and Expenditure Tracking

To meet the "cogent evidence" requirement of Sass Manufacturing and subsection 230(1) of the Act, TrenchTech integrates an Electronic Lab Notebook (ELN) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) project-code tracking system. Every design iteration is recorded contemporaneously in dated entries containing the hypothesis identifier, boundary conditions, raw sensor time-series logs, statistical regression analysis comparing predicted versus empirical soil density, and the engineering conclusion explaining why the hypothesis was falsified or validated. Shop millwrights log their hours to specific SR&ED sub-codes that cross-reference the P.Eng.'s test protocol, strictly segregating eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work from ineligible commercial chassis assembly under paragraph 248(1)(i).
Case Study 2: Industrial Food Processing & Continuous Thermal Crystallization Systems
Initial Vulnerable Project Posture (The Sass Manufacturing Trap)

A Canadian specialty food and bio-materials processor ("Chocorystallize Inc.") seeks to develop a continuous inline cold-tempering and jarring process for a novel, preservative-free cocoa butter and plant-protein emulsion spread that maintains a minimum shelf life of three to six months without artificial additives, phase separation, or fat bloom. The company's product development manager systematically tests 140 different ingredient ratios and mixing temperatures over twelve months, keeping extensive spreadsheets, graphs, tables, and written notes of batch recipes, mixing temperatures, and visual observations of texture, colour, and taste after storage.

When the CRA reviews the claim, the RTA acknowledges that the company kept extensive tables and notes of its recipe trials and that the testing was methodical, but disallows the claim in full. Relying on Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363) and subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence applying Judge Sarchuk's standard (including Soneil International Limited v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 391), the CRA concludes that while the testing was methodical, it was "simply trying to find a recipe" through empirical trial-and-error rather than conducting a systematic scientific investigation involving controlled scientific measurements of molecular crystallization.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Elevating Project Governance from Culinary Formulation to Chemical Process Engineering

The fatal flaw in Chocorystallize Inc.'s initial posture is that methodical trial-and-error ("trying 140 recipes and observing which ones stabilize") does not constitute SR&ED if it lacks an underlying scientific model explaining the physical or chemical mechanism of failure. To remediate governance, Chocorystallize Inc. places the project under the direction of a Food Process Chemist and Chemical Engineer. The project charter is restructured to prohibit blind culinary formulation trials. Instead, the technical lead defines the Technological Uncertainty at the thermodynamic and molecular level: when aqueous plant-protein micellar solutions are sheared into anhydrous cocoa butter during continuous cold-tempering, interfacial tension and latent heat release disrupt polymorphic transition from unstable Form III and Form IV crystals to stable Form V (β2) triglyceride crystals, causing rapid water migration and lipid phase instability. Standard emulsifiers and thermal profiles published in food science literature cannot resolve this thermodynamic conflict because high shear rates denature the plant proteins while low shear rates fail to nucleate Form V cocoa butter crystals.
Step 2: Restructuring Co-Development and Private Label Contracts

Suppose a national retail grocery chain has offered to contribute $150,000 toward Chocorystallize Inc.'s product development costs to secure exclusive private-label distribution rights for the resulting spread. Under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the Act, accepting this payment directly against the R&D project would trigger a contract payment or reimbursement reduction and risk characterizing the work as commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i).

To protect its SR&ED entitlement, tax counsel restructures the commercial relationship so that Chocorystallize Inc. self-funds 100% of the upstream process technology research (the continuous cold-tempering thermodynamic reactor and polymorphic nucleation process) and retains exclusive ownership of all process patents, trade secrets, and know-how. The retail chain's commercial agreement is strictly limited to a downstream Commercial Supply Purchase Order for finished jars of product at a fixed per-unit wholesale price once commercial production commences, with no right, title, or interest in the underlying SR&ED process or experimental data. Any commercial trial batches produced for consumer sensory panels or retail shelf-life validation are explicitly carved out of the SR&ED claim under paragraphs 248(1)(e) (market research or sales promotion) and 248(1)(f) (quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes).
Step 3: Replacing Qualitative Recipe Trials with Controlled Analytical Measurement

To satisfy the Sass Manufacturing and Soneil International requirements that appellants conduct controlled experiments with highly accurate measurements (Sass Manufacturing) and adopt "procedures that accorded with established and objective principles of scientific measure", Chocorystallize Inc. eliminates subjective sensory grading ("taste, texture, colour") as its experimental metric and implements an analytical laboratory protocol. Prior to each experimental series, the Chemical Engineer formulates a causal scientific hypothesis proposing that introducing a two-stage scraped-surface heat exchanger zone maintaining a shear rate of 1,500 s−1 at 28.5°C for 120 seconds, followed by ultrasonic cavitation at 20 kHz, will induce homogeneous nucleation of Form V (β2) cocoa butter polymorphs while encapsulating aqueous protein micelles below a critical droplet diameter of 10 µm, thereby binding free water and maintaining water activity (aw) below 0.60 without artificial chemical stabilizers. Experiments are executed using a structured Design of Experiments (DoE) factorial matrix where residence time, shear rate, cooling gradient (°C/min), and ultrasonic power density are varied systematically against a control batch. Every experimental run is performed in triplicate to establish statistical repeatability, directly satisfying the repeatability requirement derived from Sass Manufacturing. Instead of visual inspection, every experimental sample is analyzed using objective scientific instrumentation: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) melting thermograms measuring peak melting temperatures between 32°C and 35°C to quantify the exact percentage of Form V polymorph crystallization, Laser Diffraction Particle Size Analysis measuring Sauter mean diameter (D[3,2]) of dispersed aqueous droplets, capacitance hygrometry measuring water activity (aw) to ±0.003 precision, and oscillatory rheometry measuring storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) in Pascals.
Step 4: Audit-Ready Contemporaneous Evidence Architecture

To insulate the claim against an RTA challenge under section 5.12.1 ("Inadequate supporting evidence") of the CRA Claim Review Manual, Chocorystallize Inc. compiles a Contemporaneous SR&ED Evidence Binder for each taxation year. The binder directly maps each experimental hypothesis to its raw DSC thermogram printouts, rheology curves, statistical analysis of variance (ANOVA) tables proving variable correlation, and post-experiment analytical memoranda authored by the Chemical Engineer. In preparing Part 2 of Form T661, the technical narrative focuses exclusively on the scientific method—detailing the thermodynamic hypotheses tested, the analytical data collected, and why specific hypotheses failed—rather than emphasizing the commercial accomplishments of the finished product, thereby aligning perfectly with CRA administrative review criteria and Tax Court jurisprudence.
Synthesis of Remedial Governance Across Both Case Studies

The structural transformation required to convert an ineligible trial-and-error project into a fully defensible SR&ED claim under Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. is summarized in the following governance comparison table.

cells: Problem Definition
Framed around functional failure or commercial targets (e.g., "tamping mechanism did not perform properly"; "trying to find a recipe").
Framed around objective scientific or system-level engineering constraints that cannot be resolved by standard practice.
Experimental Methodology
Empirical trial-and-error; modifying multiple mechanical parts or recipe ratios simultaneously until the unit works.
Formal hypothesis-driven experimentation; isolating independent variables inside a controlled test environment or factorial DoE matrix.
Measurement Standard
Subjective visual inspection, pass/fail field checks, or qualitative sensory logs.
Calibrated quantitative instrumentation (e.g., kPa transducers, DSC thermograms, laser displacement sensors) ensuring scientific repeatability.
Contractual & Financial Structure
Single commercial contract for prototype fabrication with deferred customer instalment payments and an exclusivity covenant.
Legal separation of self-funded R&D from commercial sales; retention of 100% IP ownership; elimination of subsection 127(9) contract payments.
Contemporaneous Record-Keeping

Retroactive reconstruction of R&D narratives after the original returns, which did not claim the expenditures, had been filed, with no contemporaneous research logs and with limited records discarded on abandonment.
Real-time dated Electronic Lab Notebooks, hypothesis logs, raw sensor data archives, and task-specific paragraph 248(1)(d) time tracking.

body.text: Conclusion

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Sass Manufacturing Limited v. Minister of National Revenue (88 DTC 1363) remains the cornerstone of evidentiary compliance in Canadian SR&ED tax law. By establishing that Regulation 2900 (and modern subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act) requires cogent, contemporaneous evidence of controlled experiments, highly accurate measurements, and the testing of causal theories against empirical evidence, Judge Sarchuk drew an indelible legal boundary between systematic scientific investigation and empirical trial-and-error engineering. For Canadian corporations, tax counsel, and technical advisors, the enduring lesson of Sass Manufacturing is that technical complexity and commercial novelty alone cannot sustain an SR&ED claim; statutory eligibility is ultimately won or lost on the rigour of the experimental methodology, the precision of the empirical data, and the contemporaneous documentation generated while the work is underway.
